newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK manufacturers feel the pinch from pound's rally.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK manufacturers feel the pinch from pound's rally.

text.p: British manufacturers are feeling the pinch from the pound's stellar performance in recent months and few industrialists expect it to relinquish much of its gains in the months ahead.
"There has been increasing concern among manufacturers about the pound's strength," said Douglas Godden, head of the Confederation of British Industry's economic policy group.
"When it got above 2.50 marks and $1.55, worries really started to mount."

The pound's advance began in August last year. From a low of 84.0, measured against a basket of major currencies, its trade-weighted index shot up to 96.1 by the year-end, a rise of more than 14 percent.
On Wednesday, sterling was trading at 2.65 marks and $1.69, its highest level against the dollar since it ignominiously dropped out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in late 1992.
The problem for British manufacturers is that a stronger pound increases export prices, making it tougher to sell abroad.

Export market conditions are tough enough anyway, particularly in the European Union, where attempts to squeeze economies into the shape required for a single currency have pushed them to the brink of -- in some cases into -- recession.
British Prime Minister John Major weighed into the debate on Tuesday, telling a news conference a strong pound was good for subduing inflation but bad for competitiveness.
"I would be concerned if it went too far," he said, adding that he did not think that stage had been reached yet.

Godden was less sanguine, noting that the latest CBI industrial trends survey showed export orders were tailing off. "And those that are maintaining orders are only doing so by squeezing profit margins," he said.
EXPORT ORDERS FALLING

The CBI's December survey showed 15 percent more manufacturers said export orders had fallen than said orders were higher. The survey polled about 1,200 companies representing about half of Britain's manufacturing export base.
The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply's purchasing managers index also fell in December. The CIPS cited sterling's strength squeezing exports as a major factor.

Godden said larger firms could limit the risks of a higher pound by hedging currency positions in the forward and futures markets. "But smaller companies don't have access to such sophisticated instruments, or find the process too costly."
So, for many manufacturers 1997 will be a year of keeping fingers crossed and hoping the pound tumbles. Economists at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell held out little hope of that.

"Although we expect some fallback in sterling over the coming year, it is likely to be modest, if only because for much of the year the UK will be the only European country raising interest rates," they said.

The penalty for enjoying economic growth of three percent and above this year, with consumer spending likely to increase faster than that, is that interest rates are likely to head higher. That should act to push the pound higher still.
"The longer the rise in the currency is sustained, the greater an impact it will have as UK exporters will be forced to raise prices and cede market share," the DMG economists said.

Of course, a buoyant domestic economy will help to offset manufacturers' woes abroad, but Godden at the CBI said the balance of the recovery had to be reweighted in favour of exports at some stage or Britain's trade position would deteriorate fast.
"The strength of the domestic economy is balancing out the export side but it is precisely that balance of the recovery that could cause problems further out," he said.
CBI PROPOSES TAX CURB ON SPENDING

For the CBI, a more prudent policy mix would be tighter fiscal policy -- in other words higher taxes -- to give the rampant consumer pause for thought, and looser monetary policy to stop the pound in its tracks and boost investment.

But all may not be doom and gloom for Britain's beleaguered manufacturers. Roger Bootle, chief economist at HSBC Markets and one of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's independent economic advisers, said interest rates may not rise as high as the markets are forecasting.
He said the pound's rise will depress inflation as it cuts import prices and worsens the competitiveness of British industry. But if rates stay low, sterling's rally could peter out.
Britain's financial markets are pricing in base rates, now at six percent, at seven or higher by the end of the year.
And the DMG economists said the effect of the pound's storming rally will be offset to some extent by a recovery in overseas demand, particularly in the United States and Germany.

"As we saw in 1995, when UK export growth slowed despite the currency hitting an all-time low, in the short-term it is the direction of world demand growth rather than the level of the currency that tends to dominate," they said.
